chapter_theme: One song at Inthampalam (இந்தம்பலம்): a yogic hymn asking for the Sivayoga of nectar in the sky's sushumna, the Absolute of the letters and of light, and for youth and grace at the feet; the praise is a battle in drum syllables.

985.reading: The poet describes a reality no one can know: the stainless lotus form, the sounding conch and Veda, the supreme space shining everywhere, the fifty-one letters from which the worlds, rivers and cosmic eggs begin, the red light everywhere, beginning and middle, the lotus and turiya where moon and sun spread their rays, and the Sivayoga of nectar enjoyed by the five in the sushumna of the sky; he asks that, knowing it with compassion and calling 'son of Gauri, Kumara, Kumaraguru', he be given youth and grace at the feet. The praise is a battle sounded in drum syllables, the vel sent so that gods, Hari, Brahma and the sages survive, and Murugan embracing Valli, daughter of Hari, at Inthampalam.
985.nuance: The vocabulary is that of Tirumular's yoga: ககன சுழிமுனை (the sushumna in the sky of the head), துரியம், அமுத சிவயோகம், and ஐம்பந்தொரு அக்ஷரம் (the fifty-one letters). அரியின் மகள் makes Valli the daughter of Vishnu, a story the text names only in these two words. Much of the first half is a list whose syntax is uncertain.

links.note: Both lead the yogi through the sushumna to a light within; Tirumular's eight-petalled flower holds maya's city, and 985 names the nectar of Sivayoga in the sushumna of the sky as the state it asks Murugan to give.

985 names the fifty-one letters (ஐம்பந்தொரு அக்ஷரம்) as the beginning of all worlds, rivers and cosmic eggs, among the marks of the reality it asks to know. Tirumular counts the paths of the cosmos: thirty-six tattvas, mantras, fifty-one letters (வன்னம் ஐம்பான் ஒன்று), two hundred and twenty-four worlds. Both take the fifty-one letters as one of the stuffs of the world, the Tirumanthiram in a technical count, the song in a hymn.
